OIL DRILLING INDUSTRY FINAL-WAGE TIMING (LABOR CODE § 201.7) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Drilling Co.

OIL DRILLING INDUSTRY FINAL-WAGE TIMING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
California Labor Code section 201.7 sets a distinct timing rule for the payment of final wages to an employee, or a group of employees, engaged in the business of oil drilling who is laid off — a rule that operates differently from the general immediate-on-discharge deadline in Labor Code section 201 that applies to most other laid-off employees. This concerns Jordan Lee's employment with Acme Drilling Co., recorded here as ending on October 1, 2026. Section 201.7's own rule, described in the information that follows, turns on whether the work Jordan Lee performed for Acme Drilling Co. falls within the statute's description of the business of oil drilling and whether the separation was a layoff. Naming Jordan Lee and Acme Drilling Co. here does not itself determine that Jordan Lee's work was in the business of oil drilling, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular employment relationship.

THE CORE RULE: UP TO 24 HOURS (EXCLUDING WEEKENDS AND HOLIDAYS), WITH A MAILING OPTION
Labor Code section 201.7 states that an employer who lays off an employee or a group of employees engaged in the business of oil drilling is deemed to have made immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201 if the wages of those employees are paid within such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment — provided that this reasonable time may not exceed 24 hours after discharge, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. The statute further provides that this payment may be mailed, and that the date of mailing is treated as the date of payment. The statute frames this as a deeming rule tied to Section 201's own "immediate payment" requirement, rather than as a separate, freestanding due date of its own.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "An employer who lays off an employee or a group of employees engaged in the business of oil drilling shall be deemed to have made immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201 if the wages of such employees are paid within such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment thereof; provided, however, that such reasonable time shall not exceed 24 hours after discharge excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays; and provided further, such payment may be mailed and the date of mailing is the date of payment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.7 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, oil drilling layoff final-wage timing rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.7.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.7, first paragraph), used as real evidence of this section's own timing and mailing rule for a layoff of oil-drilling employees — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular employer, employee, or job duties fall within the statute's description of "the business of oil drilling," a term the statute itself does not further define. Section 201.7 by its own terms addresses only a layoff ("an employer who lays off"); its text does not say whether or how it applies to an oil-drilling employee's resignation, and this clause does not resolve that question — Labor Code section 202's 72-hour-on-quit rule, which this corpus's general final-wage-timing clause addresses, is not restated here. This clause also does not resolve what counts as "such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment," beyond the stated 24-hour outer limit; the statute does not itself define that phrase further. The single citation below is the operative text of this paragraph of Section 201.7 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

THE STATUTE'S OWN STATED REASON FOR THIS RULE
Labor Code section 201.7 recites the Legislature's own finding that special provision must be made for the payment of wages on discharge of employees engaged in oil drilling, because their employment at various locations is often far removed from the employer's principal administrative offices, which the Legislature found makes the computation and payment of wages on an immediate basis unduly burdensome.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The Legislature finds and determines that special provision must be made for the payment of wages on discharge of employees engaged in oil drilling because their employment at various locations is often far removed from the employer’s principal administrative offices, which makes the computation and payment of wages on an immediate basis unduly burdensome."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 201.7 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, oil drilling final-wage rule — legislative finding (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.7.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.7, second paragraph), presented as the statute's own recital of legislative purpose — not independent historical or legislative-history research into why the provision was enacted (it was added by Statutes 1980, Chapter 440, according to the same fetched page, but this clause does not independently verify any legislative committee analysis or bill history beyond that enactment note), and not a claim that this stated purpose determines the outcome of any particular reader's situation. The recital describes remoteness from "the employer's principal administrative offices" as the justification; the statute does not define how remote a location must be, and this clause does not supply such a definition because the fetched text of Section 201.7 does not state one. The single citation below is the operative text of this paragraph of Section 201.7 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

SECTION 203'S PENALTY LIST DOES NOT NAME SECTION 201.7 SEPARATELY
Labor Code section 203 states that if an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, wages in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, to an employee who is discharged or who quits, the employee's wages continue as a penalty from the due date at the same rate until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days. That list, as currently in force, names Section 201 but does not separately name Section 201.7. Section 201.7 itself, described elsewhere in this material, frames its 24-hour-with-mailing rule as a basis for an oil-drilling employer to be deemed to have made "immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201" — language that ties Section 201.7's own timing rule to Section 201's immediate-payment requirement, which is a section Section 203's penalty list does name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, waiting-time penalty — sections listed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=203.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 203, subdivision (a), the portion of the sentence through "30 days," quoted up to but not including the following sentence about an employee who secretes or absents themselves, which this clause does not address) and Labor Code § 201.7's own cross-reference to Section 201, used as real evidence of what each section's text currently says — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a legal conclusion about whether, or how, the Section 203 penalty applies to a late payment under Section 201.7's extended timeframe. Section 201.7 ties its own deeming rule to Section 201 rather than stating an independent penalty of its own, and Section 201 is on Section 203's list; but this clause does not resolve how that textual relationship is applied in practice, since no case law construing this specific relationship was located in the CourtListener search performed for this clause. This clause also does not restate the remainder of Section 203(a) (the secretes-or-absents-themselves exception) or Section 203(b)'s statute-of-limitations provision, which this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses generally rather than this clause duplicating them. The single citation below is the operative text of Section 203(a) as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.
